content: The double circulatory system refers to the distinct separation of pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation, which is observed in amphibians, birds, and mammals, including humans. In contrast, fish possess a single circulatory system. In humans, the adult heart functions as two separate pumps. The right side of the heart, consisting of the right atrium and right ventricle, pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary circulation, where it travels to the lungs for oxygenation. The left side of the heart, composed of the left atrium and left ventricle, pumps oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues throughout the body. Blood must pass through the heart to transition from one circuit to the other. For example, blood that has completed systemic circulation must re-enter the heart to be directed into the pulmonary circuit, and vice versa. The velocity of blood flow in the capillaries is approximately 1 cm per second. The circulatory system includes numerous return pathways, such as those to and from the kidneys, liver, and legs. Therefore, it is incorrect to assume that individual blood cells travel the entire length of the circulatory system in a single journey. On average, the human heart pumps approximately 5,040 milliliters of blood per minute. Given that the average adult has a total blood volume of about 5 liters, the heart effectively circulates the entire blood volume roughly ten times per minute.
